arXiv:2607.25018v1 [cs.LG] 27 Jul 2026

Conformal Cascade: Distribution-Free Accuracy Guarantees for Multi-Tier LLM Inference

Yifan Dou yd25b@fsu.edu Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Florida State University    Shikan Lian shikanlian@gmail.com Affiliation: -    Shibo Li shiboli@cs.fsu.edu Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Florida State University
Abstract

Large language model (LLM) cascades reduce inference cost by routing easy queries to a small model and deferring hard queries to a larger one. Production cascades govern this deferral through a confidence threshold, but LLM confidence scores are miscalibrated, the threshold must be tuned per model pair and per domain, and no setting yields a formal bound on cascade accuracy. We introduce Conformal Cascade (CC), a multi-tier inference framework that uses conformal prediction set size as the deferral rule: accept when the calibrated set collapses to a single answer, defer otherwise. The procedure delivers a distribution-free, finite-sample accuracy guarantee. By a per-tier union bound, the prediction set at the accepting tier covers the correct answer with probability at least 1−K​α1-K\alpha for any user-specified α\alpha; under a selection-preservation condition (consistent with, but not strictly implied by, our marginal coverage results), the bound tightens to 1−α1-\alpha. We further characterise expected cascade cost as an explicit function of α\alpha and the calibration-set acceptance rate. Across 18 multiple-choice benchmarks spanning science, medicine, commonsense, and standardized exams, evaluated on two-tier cascades drawn from four open-weight model families, CC strictly improves over the strongest calibration-tuned heuristic cascade on the majority of family–benchmark pairs, with the largest gains on reasoning-heavy benchmarks where majority vote is unreliable; on easier benchmarks the cascade commits the vast majority of queries to the small model at no accuracy cost. Extension to open-ended generation requires an answer-clustering step that we leave for future work. The method requires no model training and only black-box API access.

1 Introduction

Deploying large language models at scale forces a sharp trade-off between answer quality and inference cost. Serving a frontier model on every query is often prohibitive: at current token prices, inference dominates the operating expense of any high-traffic product, and each expensive call consumes accelerator time that could serve simpler queries cheaply elsewhere. LLM cascades offer the dominant production response: a query runs first on a small model, and escalates to a larger one only when needed (Chen et al., 2023; Ong et al., 2025; Aggarwal et al., 2024). What determines whether a cascade works is the deferral rule: at each tier, the decision to return the current answer or hand the query to the next model. Production cascades implement this decision as a threshold on a confidence signal such as softmax probability (Ong et al., 2025), self-consistency agreement (Wang et al., 2023; Valkanas et al., 2025), or a learned router score (Shnitzer et al., 2023): accept if the signal exceeds a cutoff θ\theta, defer otherwise.

Confidence-threshold deferral has a well-documented calibration problem. LLMs are overconfident in ways that depend on domain and input format, sharpest on the reasoning-heavy queries that benefit most from escalation (Kadavath et al., 2022; Xiong et al., 2024), and no choice of θ\theta separates confidently-wrong inputs from genuinely easy ones. The deeper issue is that the cascade’s error rate becomes an uncontrolled random variable: realized accuracy depends on the unknown joint distribution of queries, confidences, and correctness, and no analytical relationship maps a target error rate onto a threshold. Practitioners cannot answer the question that matters for deployment, “if I promise my users at most 5%5\% wrong answers, what should θ\theta be?”, and must re-sweep θ\theta on a labelled split for every new model pair, benchmark, or difficulty distribution.

We propose Conformal Cascade (CC), which replaces the confidence threshold with a conformal prediction set. At each tier, split conformal calibration (Vovk et al., 2005; Papadopoulos et al., 2002) turns a held-out labelled set into a threshold that satisfies a distribution-free coverage guarantee at that tier: for any new query, the per-tier prediction set built from this threshold contains the correct answer with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha, for a user-specified α\alpha. The size of this set, not the value of a confidence score, drives deferral. A set that collapses to a single answer declares the model conformally certain on this input, and the cascade accepts; a set with multiple candidates declares the model conformally uncertain, and the cascade escalates. Deferral cannot itself cause an error: only the acceptance event |𝒞|=1|\mathcal{C}|=1 commits a wrong answer, so the conformal guarantee binds at whichever tier the cascade commits, and per-tier guarantees compose into a cascade-level coverage bound. The calibrated threshold is fully determined by α\alpha, which reads directly as the user’s error budget, and the expected cascade cost is a closed-form function of α\alpha and the calibration-set acceptance rate.

We make three contributions. We formulate the conformal cascade for arbitrary KK tiers, where prediction-set size replaces the confidence score, and prove a cascade-level coverage bound (Theorem 2): the accepting tier’s prediction set covers the correct answer with probability at least 1−K​α1-K\alpha in the worst case, tightening to 1−α1-\alpha under a selection-preservation condition consistent with our marginal-coverage measurements. We then derive a closed-form expression for expected cascade cost as a function of α\alpha (Theorem 4). Empirically, we evaluate two-tier instantiations (K=2K=2) across four open-weight model families (Llama, Gemma, Ministral, Phi) and 18 multiple-choice benchmarks; CC strictly improves over the strongest calibration-tuned heuristic cascade on the majority of family–benchmark pairs, with the largest gains on reasoning-heavy tasks where majority vote is unreliable: examples include Ministral on MathQA, Phi on GPQA-Diamond and MedMCQA, and Gemma on TruthfulQA. The framework requires a finite, extractable answer set; extension to open-ended generation through answer clustering is left for future work. The method imposes no architectural constraints beyond self-consistency-style sampling, requires neither training nor logprob access, and exposes one interpretable hyperparameter.

2 Background and Problem Setup

Split conformal prediction.

Given a nonconformity score s:𝒳×𝒴→ℝs:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R} (lower indicates better fit), a calibration set 𝒟cal={(xi,yi)}i=1n\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} drawn exchangeably with the test point, and a target miscoverage level α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), split conformal prediction (Papadopoulos et al., 2002; Vovk et al., 2005; Lei et al., 2018; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2023) sets the threshold

q^=Quantile⁡({si}i=1n,⌈(n+1)​(1−α)⌉n)\hat{q}=\mathrm{Quantile}\!\left(\{s_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};\,\tfrac{\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil}{n}\right) (1)

and returns the prediction set 𝒞⁡(x)={y∈𝒴:s⁡(x,y)≤q^}\mathcal{C}(x)=\{y\in\mathcal{Y}:s(x,y)\leq\hat{q}\}, which satisfies the distribution-free, finite-sample guarantee:

Theorem 1 (Marginal coverage; Vovk et al., 2005).

Pr[yn+1∈𝒞(xn+1)]≥1−α\mathrm{Pr}[y_{n+1}\in\mathcal{C}(x_{n+1})]\geq 1-\alpha whenever the calibration and test points are exchangeable.

The upper bound 1−α+1/(n+1)1-\alpha+1/(n+1) holds when scores are almost surely distinct (Lei et al., 2018). Conditional coverage (per-xx at level 1−α1-\alpha) is impossible without further assumptions (Vovk, 2012; Lei and Wasserman, 2014; Foygel Barber et al., 2021).

LLM cascades.

A KK-tier LLM cascade is a sequence of models m1,…,mKm_{1},\ldots,m_{K} ordered by increasing capability and per-call cost c1<⋯<cKc_{1}<\cdots<c_{K}. Tier kk produces one or more responses; a deferral rule then decides between accepting tier kk’s answer and escalating to tier k+1k+1. If the cascade accepts at tier k∗k^{*}, the incurred cost is Cost⁡(x)=∑k=1k∗ck\mathrm{Cost}(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{k^{*}}c_{k}, since a cheap-model response is always produced before an expensive one is requested.

Problem.

For queries with a finite answer set 𝒜⁡(x)\mathcal{A}(x) (multiple choice, or extractable short answers), let ytrue∈𝒜⁡(x)y_{\mathrm{true}}\in\mathcal{A}(x) be the true answer and 𝒞k∗​(x)\mathcal{C}_{k^{*}}(x) the conformal prediction set at the accepting tier. The goal is to minimise expected inference cost 𝔼⁡[Cost⁡(X)]\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}(X)] subject to

Pr[ytrue∈𝒞k∗(X)]≥ 1−α,\mathrm{Pr}\!\left[y_{\mathrm{true}}\in\mathcal{C}_{k^{*}}(X)\right]\;\geq\;1-\alpha, (2)

where the coverage target is on the prediction set at whichever tier the cascade commits, not at a fixed tier index; this is what makes the guarantee a cascade-level statement.

3 Method

We describe each component of the Conformal Cascade. Sections 3.1–3.2 introduce the black-box nonconformity score and its per-tier calibration. Section 3.3 states the cascade algorithm. Sections 3.4–3.5 establish the cascade-level coverage guarantee and the cost–accuracy trade-off. Proofs, auxiliary lemmas, and the computational-complexity breakdown are collected in Appendix L.

The core idea is to replace the signal-plus-threshold deferral rule of Section 1 with a calibrated prediction set at each tier, whose size is the signal. A confidence threshold θ\theta has no formal tie to an error rate; the conformal threshold q^k\hat{q}_{k} has the tie supplied by Theorem 1. The user-specified parameter α\alpha then appears in two roles: as a coverage level (Theorem 2) and as a handle on expected cost (Theorem 4).

3.1 Frequency-Based Nonconformity Score

Split conformal prediction (Theorem 1) requires a real-valued nonconformity score on (x,a)(x,a) but is silent about where the score comes from. Under black-box API access, where token-level probabilities are typically not exposed, the natural choice is the sampling frequency of aa under repeated decoding from mkm_{k}. A logprob-based variant sk​(x,a)=1−pk​(a∣x)s_{k}(x,a)=1-p_{k}(a\mid x) slots into the same framework with finer resolution; we develop the frequency version because it preserves the black-box interface assumed by many production deployments and discuss the comparison to the logprob alternative in Appendix L.1.

For tier kk, we draw NN independent responses from mkm_{k} at temperature τ>0\tau>0 (the self-consistency regime of Wang et al. (2023)), giving extracted answers y^1(k),…,y^N(k)\hat{y}_{1}^{(k)},\ldots,\hat{y}_{N}^{(k)}. When the answer set 𝒜⁡(x)\mathcal{A}(x) varies per query (TruthfulQA has |𝒜⁡(x)|∈{4,…,10}|\mathcal{A}(x)|\in\{4,\ldots,10\}), all quantities below are defined per-query on 𝒜⁡(x)\mathcal{A}(x). The frequency-based nonconformity score for a∈𝒜⁡(x)a\in\mathcal{A}(x) is

sk(x,a)= 1−|{i:y^i(k)=a}|N.s_{k}(x,a)\;=\;1-\frac{\bigl|\{i:\hat{y}_{i}^{(k)}=a\}\bigr|}{N}. (3)

An answer sampled often scores low (high conformity); a rarely sampled answer scores high (low conformity). The score uses only black-box API access, reuses the NN samples already produced under self-consistency decoding, and composes naturally with a majority-vote tiebreaker when multiple answers survive calibration; its validity as a nonconformity measure follows Kumar et al. (2023). Appendix L.1 (Lemma 5) certifies that exchangeability of queries lifts to exchangeability of scores under per-query independent Monte-Carlo draws.

3.2 Per-Tier Conformal Calibration

Calibration converts the score sks_{k} into a prediction-set construction rule with a concrete coverage guarantee at level α\alpha. For each tier kk, we calibrate a threshold q^k\hat{q}_{k} on a held-out calibration set 𝒟cal={(xi,yi)}i=1n\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} by (i) drawing NN samples from mkm_{k} for each calibration query and computing si(k)=sk​(xi,yi)s_{i}^{(k)}=s_{k}(x_{i},y_{i}), (ii) sorting the scores s(1)(k)≤s(2)(k)≤⋯≤s(n)(k)s_{(1)}^{(k)}\leq s_{(2)}^{(k)}\leq\cdots\leq s_{(n)}^{(k)}, and (iii) setting q^k=s(⌈(1−α)​(n+1)⌉)(k)\hat{q}_{k}=s_{(\lceil(1-\alpha)(n+1)\rceil)}^{(k)}. The prediction set at tier kk for a new query xx is

𝒞k​(x)={a∈𝒜:sk​(x,a)≤q^k}.\mathcal{C}_{k}(x)\;=\;\{a\in\mathcal{A}:s_{k}(x,a)\leq\hat{q}_{k}\}. (4)

Operationally, q^k\hat{q}_{k} is the smallest nonconformity score the calibration set permits at coverage level α\alpha: answers scoring below it pass the conformal filter, those above are filtered out. By Theorem 1, under exchangeability Pr[ytrue∈𝒞k(x)]≥1−α\mathrm{Pr}[y_{\mathrm{true}}\in\mathcal{C}_{k}(x)]\geq 1-\alpha at each tier in isolation. Calibration-size choice, quantile tie-breaking, and computational complexity are detailed in Appendix L.2.

3.3 The Conformal Cascade Algorithm

With per-tier prediction sets in hand, the cascade asks one question at each tier: is the calibrated set small enough to commit on? Algorithm 1 specifies the procedure. An acceptance threshold κ≥1\kappa\geq 1 governs how small a set counts as a commitment (default κ=1\kappa=1).

Interpretation.

The set size measures tier-level uncertainty through the conformal filter. A set of size one (the cascade accepts, the model is conformally certain) commits to an answer; size larger than κ\kappa (conformally uncertain) escalates. An empty set is an out-of-distribution signal and is also treated as a defer. Relaxed acceptance (κ>1\kappa>1) accepts when the set is merely small, breaks argmin ties lexicographically on 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and trades a controlled amount of correctness for earlier acceptance (Section 3.5). Our implementation runs the fallback (line 11) over 𝒞K​(x)\mathcal{C}_{K}(x) when |𝒞K​(x)|≥1|\mathcal{C}_{K}(x)|\geq 1 and over 𝒜\mathcal{A} only when the tier-KK set is empty; this affects boundary behaviour on benchmarks where the cascade defers all queries but does not change the offline coverage guarantee (Appendix H).

Worked example.

Consider a 4-choice query xx on which tier-1 self-consistency draws (N=16N=16) yield extracted-answer counts {A:10,B:4,C:1,D:1}\{A:10,B:4,C:1,D:1\} and tier-1 score values s1​(x,A)=6/16,s1​(x,B)=12/16,s1​(x,C)=15/16,s1​(x,D)=15/16s_{1}(x,A)=6/16,s_{1}(x,B)=12/16,s_{1}(x,C)=15/16,s_{1}(x,D)=15/16. With a tight calibrated threshold q^1=0.50\hat{q}_{1}=0.50 (a small α\alpha), only AA passes: 𝒞1​(x)={A}\mathcal{C}_{1}(x)=\{A\}, the cascade accepts at tier 1, and the per-query cost is c1c_{1}. With a looser q^1=0.80\hat{q}_{1}=0.80, the set becomes 𝒞1​(x)={A,B}\mathcal{C}_{1}(x)=\{A,B\}: the cascade defers under κ=1\kappa=1 and pays c1+c2c_{1}+c_{2}, but with κ=2\kappa=2 it accepts and returns arg⁡mina∈{A,B}​s1​(x,a)=A\arg\min_{a\in\{A,B\}}s_{1}(x,a)=A. The same query commits at tier 1 or escalates depending on α\alpha and κ\kappa; the conformal threshold turns the raw frequency distribution into a calibrated commit/defer signal.

3.4 Theoretical Analysis

Let K∗​(x)∈{1,…,K}K^{*}(x)\in\{1,\ldots,K\} denote the first tier at which the cascade commits in Algorithm 1 (defined as KK when the fallback fires), and let A={|𝒞K∗​(x)(x)|=1}A=\{|\mathcal{C}_{K^{*}(x)}(x)|=1\} be the acceptance event.

Theorem 2 (Cascade coverage).

Let (x,ytrue)(x,y_{\mathrm{true}}) be exchangeable with each tier-kk calibration set, for k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K. In a KK-tier Conformal Cascade with per-tier level α\alpha and acceptance parameter κ=1\kappa=1,

Pr⁡[y^≠ytrue,A]≤K⋅α,\mathrm{Pr}\!\left[\,\hat{y}\neq y_{\mathrm{true}},\,A\,\right]\;\leq\;K\cdot\alpha, (5)

so per-tier level α/K\alpha/K ensures cascade error at most α\alpha.

The proof partitions AA into the KK disjoint first-commit events Ak={K∗(x)=k}A_{k}=\{K^{*}(x)=k\} and applies Theorem 1 on each (Appendix L.3). Two facts about the bound matter for practice. Deferral cannot itself cause an error: only the acceptance event AA commits a wrong answer, escalation only incurs additional cost, and the cascade error decomposes over the disjoint commit events {Ak}k=1K\{A_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}. Per-tier guarantees therefore compose into a cascade-level bound by a union bound on these disjoint events. The factor KK is the union-bound worst case; tighter statements hold under selective-inference conditions (Bates et al., 2023; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2023), captured by the next assumption.

Assumption 3 (Selection preservation).

For each tier kk, Pr⁡[ytrue∈𝒞k​(x)∣K∗​(x)=k]≥1−α\mathrm{Pr}[\,y_{\mathrm{true}}\in\mathcal{C}_{k}(x)\mid K^{*}(x)=k\,]\geq 1-\alpha.

Under Assumption 3 the cascade error is bounded by α\alpha directly. The first-commit event {K∗(x)=k}\{K^{*}(x)=k\} is label-free—a function of xx and the calibration scores, not ytruey_{\mathrm{true}}—which places it in the family studied by selective conformal inference; the assumption asks that this label-free selection preserve per-tier coverage, and is not derivable from split CP alone. Section 5.3 reports marginal miscoverage tracking α\alpha rather than K​αK\alpha, which rules out the K​αK\alpha bound being tight here but is only consistent with, not strictly implied by, Assumption 3 (which would require per-tier conditional miscoverage). Two further notes on scope: Theorem 2 bounds the joint event {error, acceptance}; on the fallback path the cascade returns an argmin without an active conformal commit and inherits no per-tier guarantee (rare in practice—Appendix H). For κ>1\kappa>1 the union bound controls set coverage, and the top-1 error picks up an additional slack from the argmin tiebreaker (Remark 8, Appendix L.3). The relaxed-acceptance variant and the heterogeneous-αk\alpha_{k} extension are also in Appendix L.3.

3.5 Cost–Coverage Trade-off

The accuracy guarantee comes paired with a closed-form expression for expected cost.

Theorem 4 (Cost–coverage, two-tier).

For a two-tier cascade (K=2)(K=2) with costs c1<c2c_{1}<c_{2} and κ=1\kappa=1,

𝔼[Cost(X)]=c1+c2⋅Pr[|𝒞1(X)|≠1].\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}(X)]\;=\;c_{1}+c_{2}\cdot\mathrm{Pr}\!\left[\,|\mathcal{C}_{1}(X)|\neq 1\,\right]. (6)

Expected cost depends only on the calibration-set non-acceptance rate, which is observable on labelled calibration data without further test queries. The asymptotes are clean: as α→0\alpha\to 0 prediction sets grow and cost approaches c1+c2c_{1}+c_{2}; as α→1\alpha\to 1 sets shrink to singletons and cost approaches c1c_{1}. Cost is monotone in α\alpha on the admissible range, and the cascade strictly improves over the always-defer baseline (𝔼⁡[Cost]<c1+c2\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}]<c_{1}+c_{2}) whenever the cheap model produces any singleton sets on calibration (Proposition 10). Improving over Always-Strong (which skips tier 1 and pays c2c_{2}) requires the stricter condition Pr[|𝒞1(X)|=1]>c1/c2\mathrm{Pr}[|\mathcal{C}_{1}(X)|=1]>c_{1}/c_{2}, since the cascade pays c1c_{1} per query for the tier-1 samples regardless of whether they trigger acceptance.

For K>2K>2 tiers, 𝔼⁡[Cost⁡(X)]=∑k=1K(∑j=1kcj)⋅pk\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}(X)]=\sum_{k=1}^{K}(\sum_{j=1}^{k}c_{j})\cdot p_{k} with pk=Pr[K∗(X)=k]p_{k}=\mathrm{Pr}[K^{*}(X)=k] (Corollary 11, appendix). Combined with Theorem 2, this gives a practitioner recipe: for a target cascade error rate β\beta, set α=β/K\alpha=\beta/K in the worst case or α=β\alpha=\beta under Assumption 3 as a deployment heuristic (Remark 12, appendix; finite-NN monotonicity is checked by a small calibration sweep, Appendix J). The user fixes the error budget; the cascade picks the threshold.

Concretely, with K=2K=2 and c1=1c_{1}=1, c2=2.7c_{2}=2.7, an 80%80\% calibration acceptance rate gives 𝔼⁡[Cost]=1.54\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}]=1.54 (43%43\% saving over Always-Strong); the saving as a function of cost ratio r=c2/c1r=c_{2}/c_{1} is in Appendix J.

4 Related Work

Split conformal prediction (Vovk et al., 2005; Papadopoulos et al., 2002; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2023; Shafer and Vovk, 2008) produces prediction sets with distribution-free finite-sample coverage and has been extended to regression (Romano et al., 2019; Lei et al., 2018), classification with adaptive coverage (Romano et al., 2020; Angelopoulos et al., 2021), jackknife-style resampling (Barber et al., 2021), and covariate shift (Tibshirani et al., 2019; Gibbs and Candès, 2021; Angelopoulos et al., 2023). Recent LLM-specific variants address the settings where standard scores fail: sampling-frequency nonconformity when logprobs are unavailable (Kumar et al., 2023), conformal stopping rules for open-ended generation (Quach et al., 2024; Deutschmann et al., 2024), conformal factuality for free-form generation (Mohri and Hashimoto, 2024; Cherian et al., 2024), and conformal binary routing between a base LLM and a reasoning model (Su et al., 2026). These methods cover single-model or two-model settings; none constructs conformal sets at every tier of a cascade, uses set size as the deferral criterion, or proves coverage composition across tiers. On the cascade side, heuristic-threshold methods (Chen et al., 2023; Aggarwal et al., 2024), preference-learned routers (Ong et al., 2025; Ding et al., 2024), benchmark-trained routers (Shnitzer et al., 2023), mixture-of-thought cascades (Yue et al., 2024), and theoretical analyses of confidence-based cascade deferral (Jitkrittum et al., 2023; Dohan et al., 2022) form the current production and analytical landscape; none of these provides a distribution-free finite-sample accuracy guarantee that holds at every tier, and each requires labelled data to tune per deployment.

Comparison to C3PO.

The closest prior work is C3PO (Valkanas et al., 2025), also a conformal-prediction approach to LLM cascades but on an orthogonal axis: C3PO bounds the probability that per-query inference cost exceeds a budget (Pr[cost>C∗]≤α\Pr[\mathrm{cost}>C^{*}]\leq\alpha) using a confidence-threshold deferral rule and self-supervised calibration, whereas CC bounds the probability that the accepting tier’s set misses the correct answer using a binary set-size test and labelled calibration. C3PO suits a fixed compute budget seeking cost control; CC suits a fixed error budget seeking accuracy control. Appendix A gives the row-by-row design contrast.

Underneath these threshold-based cascades lies a calibration problem: neural-network confidence is systematically miscalibrated (Guo et al., 2017), and elicited LLM confidence in particular drifts on reasoning tasks (Kadavath et al., 2022; Xiong et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2022a; Tian et al., 2023; Kuhn et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024). Classical post-hoc rescaling (Platt scaling, temperature scaling) adjusts score magnitudes without restoring a distribution-free guarantee, whereas conformal prediction sidesteps calibration by bounding set-level coverage directly. Beyond calibration, adaptive compute allocation at inference time is an active area: Snell et al. (2025) show that the optimal allocation depends on query difficulty, Setlur et al. (2025) argue that verification-based strategies outperform verification-free sampling, and Lightman et al. (2024) show that verifiers trained at the step level can substantially improve reasoning reliability; CC is verification-based in this sense, with the verifier being a conformal set-size check whose correctness carries a distribution-free guarantee. Our frequency-based score builds on self-consistency decoding (Wang et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024), which is itself part of the chain-of-thought family (Wei et al., 2022).

5 Experiments

5.1 Setup

Models.

We evaluate two-tier (K=2K=2) cascades drawn from four open-weight instruction-tuned families: Llama (Llama Team, 2024), Gemma (Gemma Team, 2024), Ministral (Mistral AI Team, 2024), and Phi (Abdin et al., 2024); while the framework supports arbitrary KK, the empirical sweep is restricted to K=2K=2. Tier 1 is the smallest public instruction-tuned checkpoint; tier 2 is a substantially larger checkpoint from the same family (identifiers in Appendix B). For each query we draw N=16N=16 samples at temperature τ=0.7\tau=0.7 from each tier via vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023). Per-call costs are fixed at c1=1c_{1}=1, c2=2.7c_{2}=2.7 across all four families; sensitivity to alternative c2/c1c_{2}/c_{1} is in Appendix J.

Benchmarks.

We evaluate on 18 multiple-choice benchmarks covering science (Welbl et al., 2017; Khot et al., 2020; Clark et al., 2018; Rein et al., 2024), medicine (Pal et al., 2022; Jin et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2019), broad knowledge (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024), commonsense (Zellers et al., 2019; Bisk et al., 2020; Sap et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019; Clark et al., 2019), factuality (Lin et al., 2022b), standardized exams (Zhong et al., 2024), mathematics (Amini et al., 2019), and multilingual reading (Bandarkar et al., 2024). Answer sets range from four to ten options. Each benchmark splits 30%/70%30\%/70\% calibration/test with seed 4242, giving 72 family–benchmark pairs; full statistics in Table 6.

Baselines.

CC is compared against five label-light deferral rules that share its sample budget: (1) Always-Weak and (2) Always-Strong (majority vote at the corresponding tier, no tuning); (3) Agreement cascade, deferring if tier-1 top-answer agreement is below θ∈{0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9}\theta\in\{0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9\}; (4) Entropy cascade, τ∈{−1.5,−1.0,−0.5,−0.3}\tau\in\{-1.5,-1.0,-0.5,-0.3\}; (5) Random defer, p∈{0.2,0.5,0.8}p\in\{0.2,0.5,0.8\}. The heuristic grid contains 12 tunable configurations. Learned routers (Ong et al., 2025; Shnitzer et al., 2023; Ding et al., 2024) require labelled preference data and a separate parametric scorer outside CC’s calibration regime; we discuss them in Section 4 but do not run them as direct baselines.

CC and reporting protocol.

CC is evaluated over a 15-point grid: α∈{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20,0.30}\alpha\in\{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20,0.30\} and κ∈{1,2,3}\kappa\in\{1,2,3\}. For each family–benchmark pair, Best Heuristic is the argmax test-set accuracy over the 12-configuration heuristic grid; CC Best is the argmax over the 15-configuration CC grid. Both methods are thus reported at oracle-tuned operating points per benchmark, on grids of comparable size. Coverage (Table 2, Appendix I) and tier-1 acceptance (Table 3, Appendix E) are reported at the tuning-free anchor α=0.10,κ=1\alpha=0.10,\kappa=1, where α\alpha reads as the user’s error budget.

5.2 CC strictly improves over heuristic cascades on accuracy

Table 1 reports the per-benchmark, per-family accuracy gap Δ=CC Best−Best Heuristic\Delta=\text{CC Best}-\text{Best Heuristic} across the 72 evaluated pairs at oracle-tuned operating points (both methods test-set argmax over their hyperparameter grids; deployment-time numbers at fixed α=0.10\alpha{=}0.10, κ=1\kappa{=}1 are in Tables 2, 3). CC strictly improves on 49 pairs, ties within 0.050.05 pp on 6, and underperforms on 17. The six largest gains are Ministral/MathQA (+4.6+4.6), Phi/GPQA-Diamond (+4.3+4.3), Phi/MedMCQA (+3.6+3.6), Gemma/TruthfulQA (+3.3+3.3), Gemma/MedMCQA (+3.0+3.0), and Gemma/MedQA-USMLE-4 (+2.8+2.8). Every family has at least one gain ≥+1.5\geq+1.5 pp, and all four families win the majority of their benchmarks. Full absolute accuracies are in Appendix C.

Where the method is weaker.

Phi is the outlier on the losing side: large wins on reasoning and medicine (Phi/GPQA-Diamond +4.3+4.3, Phi/MedMCQA +3.6+3.6), but −4.5-4.5 pp on AGI-Eval and −1.4-1.4 pp on both MathQA and PubmedQA. The failure mode is diagnosable from the tier-1 set-size distribution (Section 5.5): on these benchmarks the Phi mini checkpoint spreads sampling probability so broadly that every tier-1 conformal set retains all (or nearly all) answer choices, the cascade defers 100%100\% of queries to tier 2, and the cascade’s fallback selection rule under-performs Always-Strong’s unrestricted majority on the same tier-2 samples (e.g., 45.7%45.7\% vs 51.0%51.0\% on Phi/AGI-Eval; see Appendix H). CC is most useful when the cheap model’s sampling distribution is concentrated enough to commit at tier 1 on easy queries and bimodal-or-narrow on hard queries to leave a small conformal set; uniformly diffuse tier-1 distributions, like Phi on AGI-Eval, eliminate both modes.

5.3 The coverage guarantee holds empirically

Table 2 reports the empirical set-miscoverage rate Pr[ytrue∉𝒞K∗​(x)(x)]\mathrm{Pr}[y_{\mathrm{true}}\notin\mathcal{C}_{K^{*}(x)}(x)] for CC-Offline at α∈{0.05,0.10,0.20,0.30}\alpha\in\{0.05,0.10,0.20,0.30\} on the Llama cascade. At α=0.10\alpha=0.10, six of eight benchmarks meet the strict target within the ±0.02\pm 0.02 finite-sample band; MedMCQA at 0.1300.130 and ARC-Challenge at 0.1240.124 exceed strict α\alpha by margins that are statistically significant given their test-set sizes (5.4σ\sigma and 2.3σ\sigma, respectively), but both remain comfortably inside the worst-case K​α=0.20K\alpha=0.20 bound of Theorem 2. The same pattern (small overshoot at strict α\alpha, well within K​αK\alpha) holds on five additional cells across the other three families (Appendix I marks them with ∗); every reported cell satisfies the union bound. The empirical regime is therefore between α\alpha and K​αK\alpha, closer to the former. This rules out the worst-case K​αK\alpha bound being tight in our setting; it is consistent with, but does not directly verify, Assumption 3, which would require the per-tier conditional miscoverage breakdown that our aggregate logs do not retain (Section 3.4). Results for the other three families are in Appendix I.

5.4 The cost–accuracy Pareto frontier

Accuracy at the best-α\alpha operating point is only part of the story. In production, the practitioner-facing question is how CC trades cost for accuracy across a range of operating points. Figure 1 plots the cost–accuracy scatter on MMLU for three of the four cascades (Llama, Gemma, Ministral), sweeping every hyperparameter of every method; the Phi panel is in Appendix D.

On Llama, CC (κ=1\kappa=1) sits strictly above every heuristic for expected cost ≥1.5\geq 1.5 (e.g., at cost 2.862.86, 75.1%75.1\% vs Always-Strong’s 74.8%74.8\% at 2.702.70); on Ministral, CC dominates Agreement across the mid-cost range (e.g., 83.7%83.7\% at cost 2.012.01 vs Agree(θ=0.8\theta=0.8)’s 82.5%82.5\% at 1.971.97); on Gemma, where tier-1 already hits 82.6%82.6\%, headroom is smaller and CC matches or slightly exceeds the heuristic frontier. Relaxing κ\kappa to {2,3}\{2,3\} accepts earlier and trades within-set selection accuracy for lower cost, moving along a second Pareto axis that no single agreement or entropy threshold tracks. Full per-family curves for the remaining 17 benchmarks are in Appendix D.

5.5 Where the gains come from

Where in the data does CC’s advantage concentrate? Two stratifications give complementary views. A difficulty breakdown on MMLU-Pro (Llama, α=0.10\alpha=0.10, 100%100\% deferral to tier 2) shows CC’s gap over Always-Strong sitting on the hard bucket: 7.2%7.2\% versus 3.4%3.4\% on queries where the strong model’s per-query accuracy p^<0.25\hat{p}<0.25, a +3.8+3.8 pp gain. On the easy and medium buckets the methods sit within 0.50.5 pp of each other. The same hard-bucket-concentrated pattern holds on Ministral/MMLU and Ministral/MMLU-Pro (CC ahead by 44–66 pp on hard queries); on Gemma/MMLU-Pro the strong model bottoms out at 0%0\% on hard queries and CC has no headroom to recover. Full per-bucket numbers for all four cells are in Appendix G.

The second view is the tier-1 prediction-set distribution. Table 3 reports the tier-1 acceptance rate (|𝒞1|=1|\mathcal{C}_{1}|=1) and median set size at α=0.10\alpha=0.10 on the Llama cascade. Acceptance ranges from 0%0\% on MMLU-Pro and GPQA-Diamond (all queries defer) to 95.6%95.6\% on Belebele-Eng (almost all queries commit at tier 1): the cascade automatically routes benchmarks where the small model is reliable to tier 1 and defers the rest, without per-benchmark tuning.

Diagnosing failures.

On Phi/AGI-Eval (Δ=−4.5\Delta=-4.5 pp), the tier-1 conformal sets never collapse to a singleton at any tested α\alpha, the cascade defers 100%100\% of queries, and the gap to Always-Strong comes from the fallback selection rule (Appendix H).

6 Discussion

Deployment recipe.

Setup is three steps: hold out a labelled calibration split per tier (n≥200n\geq 200 recommended), draw NN self-consistency samples per calibration query at the production temperature and store q^k\hat{q}_{k}, and at inference run Algorithm 1. The practitioner picks β\beta and sets α=β/K\alpha=\beta/K in the worst case or α=β\alpha=\beta under Assumption 3. A label-free guard rail handles the diffuse-tier-1 regime (Phi/AGI-Eval, Section 5.5): if calibration tier-1 acceptance falls below the break-even rate 1/r1/r (r=c2/c1r=c_{2}/c_{1}; r=2.7r=2.7 here gives 1/r≈0.371/r\approx 0.37, larger production ratios push it lower; Appendix J), replacing CC with Always-Strong saves c1c_{1} per query at no accuracy cost.

Scope, limitations, and impact.

The guarantee is marginal, not conditional on query difficulty; strengthening this is a known hard problem. Calibration–test exchangeability comes from within-benchmark splitting, so covariate-shift deployment needs online recalibration. The framework requires a finite extractable answer set; open-ended generation needs an answer-clustering step. Aggregate-only logs preclude bootstrap intervals; small differences (|Δ|<0.5|\Delta|<0.5 pp on GPQA-Diamond at ntest=139n_{\text{test}}=139) are point estimates. The auditable error budget reduces per-query compute when the small model is reliable, but the marginal guarantee gives no subgroup protection and base-model disparities pass through; high-stakes deployments should pair CC with subgroup-conditioned calibration and content-safety tooling.

Appendix D Full Per-Family Pareto Frontiers

Figure 1 in the main body shows the MMLU Pareto frontier for three of the four cascades; the Phi panel is qualitatively similar and is omitted from the figure for visual readability. A full per-benchmark Pareto visualisation across all 72 family–benchmark pairs is released with the code. The qualitative pattern on MMLU repeats across benchmarks: CC (κ=1\kappa=1) sits on or above the heuristic frontier in the mid- to high-cost region on most benchmarks, while relaxed-acceptance variants κ∈{2,3}\kappa\in\{2,3\} extend the frontier downward into the low-cost region that heuristics can only reach by sacrificing the coverage guarantee. Appendix E Full Set-Size Distributions

Table 8 reports the tier-1 acceptance rate (the fraction of test queries with |𝒞1​(x)|=1|\mathcal{C}_{1}(x)|=1) at α=0.10\alpha=0.10 across the 72 family–benchmark pairs, extracted directly from the experiment logs. Rows are ordered by mean acceptance across families. The table makes the cascade’s partitioning behaviour concrete: the same α=0.10\alpha=0.10 threshold produces acceptance rates ranging from 0%0\% (cascade defers every query) to over 95%95\% (cascade commits nearly every query). The acceptance rate varies strongly across benchmarks within a family and across families within a benchmark, tracking the tier-1 model’s per-benchmark confidence.

Two observations are worth flagging. First, the cascade never accepts at tier 1 on GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro, AGI-Eval, TruthfulQA, or PubmedQA for any family at α=0.10\alpha=0.10: these are benchmarks on which tier-1 sampling is broadly uncertain, and the cascade correctly defers everything. Second, Phi has zero or near-zero acceptance on 14 of 18 benchmarks; this pattern correlates with Phi’s weaker performance on the negative-Δ\Delta benchmarks in Table 1 (see Appendix H).

Appendix F Why CC Outperforms Majority Vote

The conformal set acts as a calibrated frequency filter. On benchmarks with many answer choices (MMLU-Pro has 10), the correct answer often receives only 4–6 of the 16 samples while incorrect answers fragment across the remaining nine alternatives. Majority vote is easy to beat in this regime: two wrong answers with three votes each can outvote the correct answer with four. The conformal threshold removes low-frequency answers, denoising the vote at a calibration-guaranteed rate.

Appendix G Difficulty Stratification

Table 9 expands the difficulty breakdown summarised in Section 5.5 to four (family, benchmark) cells. Buckets follow the raw evaluation: easy queries have tier-2 per-query accuracy p^≥0.6\hat{p}\geq 0.6, medium 0.25≤p^<0.60.25\leq\hat{p}<0.6, hard p^<0.25\hat{p}<0.25. These four cells split into two regimes that we analyse separately (Table 8). On the MMLU-Pro rows the tier-1 acceptance rate at α=0.10\alpha=0.10 is 0%0\%, so the cascade defers every query and CC reduces to post-hoc conformal selection over the tier-2 candidate set. On the MMLU rows the tier-1 acceptance is 78.7%78.7\% (Gemma) and 62.7%62.7\% (Ministral), so CC is doing both routing and, on the deferred subset, conformal selection.

Pure-selection regime (MMLU-Pro cells).

All rows here operate on the same tier-2 samples; differences come entirely from how each method selects among the strong model’s candidates. Against Always-Strong, CC gains +3.8+3.8 pp on Llama/MMLU-Pro hard (7.2%7.2\% vs. 3.4%3.4\%) and +4.4+4.4 pp on Ministral/MMLU-Pro hard (4.7%4.7\% vs. 0.3%0.3\%): the conformal filter retains the correct answer in a multi-element set, and the argmin-frequency tiebreaker over the calibrated set picks more reliably than the strong model’s argmax when that argmax is wrong. Against unrestricted majority (Agreement, θ=0.8\theta=0.8), CC gains +3.3+3.3 pp and +2.8+2.8 pp on the hard buckets of these two cells respectively. The easy-bucket cost relative to Always-Strong is at most 0.60.6 pp, since on p^≥0.6\hat{p}\geq 0.6 queries the strong-model argmax is rarely overturned by the tiebreaker.

Routing + selection regime (MMLU cells).

On these cells CC’s accuracy is a mixture of the small model on accepted queries and the conformally filtered cascade on deferred queries, and deferral is concentrated on hard queries: although the overall tier-1 acceptance is 78.7%78.7\%/62.7%62.7\%, the cascade defers more often when the small model is uncertain, which on these cells coincides with queries where the strong model also fails (Always-Strong hard accuracy is 0.0%0.0\% on both cells). The bucket-level effect is asymmetric:

  • •

    Easy. CC (96.1%96.1\% on Gemma/MMLU, 98.9%98.9\% on Ministral/MMLU) sits between Always-Weak (88.6%88.6\%, 90.4%90.4\%) and Always-Strong (100.0%100.0\%, 100.0%100.0\%): selective deferral catches part of the small model’s easy-bucket error mass without forcing every query through the strong model.

  • •

    Hard. CC (5.5%5.5\%, 6.4%6.4\%) lies much closer to Always-Strong (0.0%0.0\%, 0.0%0.0\%) than to Always-Weak (19.1%19.1\%, 14.3%14.3\%). The cascade defers the bulk of hard queries to a strong model that is wrong on essentially all of them, and conformal selection cannot recover what is not in the candidate set; the +5.5+5.5/+6.4+6.4 pp the filter extracts over Always-Strong is what is available given that recall constraint.

Cross-regime takeaway.

Always-Weak has the highest hard-bucket accuracy on all four cells. This is not in tension with the cascade’s value but a predictable consequence of two facts: difficulty is defined by the strong model’s per-query accuracy, so queries hard for the strong model are not always hard for the small model; and on the MMLU cells the strong model’s hard bucket collapses to 0%0\%, leaving Always-Weak with structurally unrecoverable headroom. On MMLU cells the cascade therefore trades a hard-bucket loss for higher overall accuracy and calibrated coverage; on MMLU-Pro cells, where the small model never accepts, CC delivers a strict hard-bucket improvement over Always-Strong at ≤0.6\leq 0.6 pp easy-bucket cost. The four cells reflect properties of the (family, benchmark) pair, not an inconsistency in CC’s deferral rule, which targets the same calibrated risk throughout.

Appendix H Failure Diagnostics: Phi’s Under-Performance

Phi is the cascade with the most negative-Δ\Delta benchmarks (Table 1: 12 wins, 0 ties, 6 losses, with Δ≤−1\Delta\leq-1 pp on 3 benchmarks: AGI-Eval, MathQA, PubmedQA). The most visible failure is AGI-Eval at Δ=−4.5\Delta=-4.5 pp. The raw logs reveal a consistent pattern: on the benchmarks where Phi under-performs, the Phi tier-1 model produces prediction sets that saturate toward the full answer set at α≤0.20\alpha\leq 0.20, which forces CC to defer 100%100\% of queries to tier 2 (defer rate =100.0%=100.0\%, cost = c1+c2=3.70c_{1}+c_{2}=3.70). At the committed tier-2 output, the cascade’s accuracy is then lower than Always-Strong’s accuracy on the same benchmark (e.g., on Phi/AGI-Eval: all CC variants achieve 45.7%45.7\% accuracy versus 51.0%51.0\% for Always-Strong). The gap arises from a design choice in the fallback rule: when CC reaches the last tier with a non-singleton prediction set, it returns the argmin frequency answer within the tier-KK set rather than the unrestricted majority vote, and the two decisions disagree exactly when the tier-KK set is itself non-singleton. An alternative fallback that takes the argmax frequency over tier-KK samples without conditioning on the tier-KK set would recover Always-Strong accuracy under full deferral. We use the more conservative fallback throughout the experiments and note the alternative as an implementation choice that affects boundary behaviour but not the offline coverage guarantee of Theorem 2.

The Phi tier-1 saturation itself is a property of the Phi-3.5-mini-instruct checkpoint at N=16N=16: on benchmarks where the mini model is uniformly uncertain, the frequency-based score produces broad sets that never meet the singleton acceptance criterion, and the cascade cannot exit at tier 1. Switching to a logprob-based score or increasing NN would sharpen the sets but neither addresses the underlying tier-1 uncertainty. The simplest practical fix is to detect this regime on calibration data (tier-1 acceptance rate close to 0%0\%) and fall back to Always-Strong.

Appendix J Cost-Ratio Sensitivity

The main paper fixes the per-call cost ratio at c2/c1=2.7c_{2}/c_{1}=2.7 across all four families to decouple cross-family comparisons from provider-specific pricing. Real ratios vary: closed-API pricing for small/large model pairs typically gives c2/c1∈[3,50]c_{2}/c_{1}\in[3,50], with reasoning-tuned models at the high end. Theorem 4 expresses expected cost as 𝔼[Cost]=c1+c2⋅Pr[|𝒞1(X)|≠1]\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}]=c_{1}+c_{2}\cdot\mathrm{Pr}[|\mathcal{C}_{1}(X)|\neq 1], so for any acceptance rate p=Pr[|𝒞1(X)|=1]p=\mathrm{Pr}[|\mathcal{C}_{1}(X)|=1] the cost reduction relative to Always-Strong (which pays c2c_{2}) is

Saving⁡(p,r)=c2−(c1+c2​(1−p))c2=p−1r,r:=c2/c1,\mathrm{Saving}(p,r)\;=\;\frac{c_{2}-(c_{1}+c_{2}(1-p))}{c_{2}}\;=\;p-\frac{1}{r},\qquad r\;:=\;c_{2}/c_{1},

and CC saves cost over Always-Strong if and only if p>1/rp>1/r. The same expression rewritten as Saving⁡(p,r)=p⋅r−1/p⋅(1−p)r\mathrm{Saving}(p,r)=p\cdot\frac{r-1/p\cdot(1-p)}{r} shows that as rr grows, the threshold acceptance rate 1/r1/r shrinks toward zero and saving asymptotes at pp.

Two qualitative consequences for deployment. First, the larger the cost gap between cheap and expensive models (i.e., the more economically meaningful a cascade is), the lower the acceptance threshold for CC to save cost. At r=10r=10 (typical of small/frontier model pairs), even 20%20\% tier-1 acceptance produces a 10%10\% saving over Always-Strong; at r=50r=50, 5%5\% acceptance suffices. Second, the cost figures reported in the main paper at r=2.7r=2.7 are conservative: on Llama/Belebele-Eng with p=0.956p=0.956, the saving rises from 58%58\% at r=2.7r=2.7 to 86%86\% at r=10r=10 and 94%94\% at r=50r=50. The diffuse-tier-1 guard rail discussed in Section 6 (replace CC with Always-Strong when calibration acceptance is below 1/r1/r) is therefore a function of the deployment cost ratio rather than a fixed 5%5\% rule.

Appendix K Algorithm and Implementation Details

Sampling.

All experiments use temperature τ=0.7\tau=0.7 and N=16N=16 samples. For multiple-choice benchmarks we extract the answer letter from the first token of the response, falling back to regex extraction on the body. Malformed responses contribute to no candidate and thus score sk​(x,a)=1s_{k}(x,a)=1 for every aa, which produces a maximal set and defers.

Calibration.

We use a 30%/70%30\%/70\% calibration/test split with fixed seed 42. The conformal quantile in Eq. (1) is implemented by sorting the calibration scores and indexing at position ⌈(1−α)​(n+1)⌉\lceil(1-\alpha)(n+1)\rceil; ties are broken by preserving the sort order, which makes the quantile conservative.

Baselines and selection.

The agreement cascade is swept over θ∈{0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9}\theta\in\{0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9\}; the entropy cascade over τ∈{−1.5,−1.0,−0.5,−0.3}\tau\in\{-1.5,-1.0,-0.5,-0.3\}; the random-defer baseline over p∈{0.2,0.5,0.8}p\in\{0.2,0.5,0.8\}. For each family–benchmark pair, Best Heuristic is the argmax test-set accuracy over the resulting 12 configurations, and CC Best is the argmax test-set accuracy over the 15-configuration CC grid (5​α×3​κ5\,\alpha\times 3\,\kappa from Section 5.1); the same oracle-tuning rule is applied on both sides. Coverage and tier-1 acceptance results in the main paper are reported at the fixed operating point α=0.10,κ=1\alpha=0.10,\kappa=1 without per-benchmark selection.

Compute.

The full evaluation (four families ×\times 18 benchmarks ×\times N=16N=16 samples per tier per query) runs on four NVIDIA B200 SXM6 GPUs. Conformal calibration itself is negligible—a sort and an index per tier.

Appendix L Proofs and Technical Details for Section 3

This appendix collects the formal material referenced from Section 3. Subsection L.1 certifies that the Monte-Carlo-based nonconformity score inherits exchangeability from the underlying queries (Lemma 5) and discusses the resolution of the score. Subsection L.2 spells out the computational cost and calibration-size recommendations for the per-tier calibration. Subsections L.3 and L.4 contain the proofs of the two main theorems (Theorem 2 and Theorem 4), the auxiliary results cited from the main body, and additional remarks. Subsection L.5 gives the end-to-end computational-complexity breakdown of Algorithm 1.

L.1 Score-Level Exchangeability and Resolution

The main body states two properties of the frequency score sks_{k} (Section 3.1) that drive its use inside split conformal prediction. We record both formally here.

Validity through exchangeability.

The split conformal guarantee (Theorem 1) requires the calibration and test points to produce exchangeable nonconformity scores. Our score sks_{k} is stochastic in the Monte-Carlo samples drawn from mkm_{k}, so this is not immediate: in principle, the randomness of the draws could break the joint exchangeability of the score vector even when the query sequence is exchangeable. The following Lemma establishes that this concern does not materialize.

Lemma 5 (Exchangeability of frequency scores).

Let (x1,ytrue(1)),…,(xn,ytrue(n)),(xn+1,ytrue(n+1))(x_{1},y_{\mathrm{true}}^{(1)}),\ldots,(x_{n},y_{\mathrm{true}}^{(n)}),(x_{n+1},y_{\mathrm{true}}^{(n+1)}) be an exchangeable sequence of query–answer pairs. For each tier kk and each index ii, let Zi(k)=(y^i,1(k),…,y^i,N(k))Z_{i}^{(k)}=(\hat{y}_{i,1}^{(k)},\ldots,\hat{y}_{i,N}^{(k)}) denote the NN Monte Carlo samples drawn from mkm_{k} on xix_{i}, and assume that the conditional law of Zi(k)Z_{i}^{(k)} given xix_{i} is the same measurable kernel Pk(⋅∣⋅)P_{k}(\cdot\mid\cdot) for every ii (so that Zi(k)∣xi∼Pk(⋅∣xi)Z_{i}^{(k)}\mid x_{i}\sim P_{k}(\cdot\mid x_{i}) identically across queries) and that the draws {Zi(k)}i\{Z_{i}^{(k)}\}_{i} are mutually independent given {xi}i\{x_{i}\}_{i}. Then the tier-kk frequency scores {sk​(xi,ytrue(i))}i=1n+1\{s_{k}(x_{i},y_{\mathrm{true}}^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^{n+1} are exchangeable.

Proof.

Each score can be written as sk​(xi,ytrue(i))=f⁡(xi,ytrue(i),Zi(k))s_{k}(x_{i},y_{\mathrm{true}}^{(i)})=f(x_{i},y_{\mathrm{true}}^{(i)},Z_{i}^{(k)}), where the deterministic measurable function f:𝒳×𝒜×𝒜N→[0,1]f:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{A}^{N}\to[0,1] is defined by

f(x,a,z)= 1−1N∑j=1N𝟙[zj=a].f(x,a,z)\;=\;1-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbb{1}[z_{j}=a].

Consider the augmented sequence Wi=(xi,ytrue(i),Zi(k))W_{i}=(x_{i},y_{\mathrm{true}}^{(i)},Z_{i}^{(k)}) for i=1,…,n+1i=1,\ldots,n+1. By assumption, {(xi,ytrue(i))}\{(x_{i},y_{\mathrm{true}}^{(i)})\} is exchangeable and {Zi(k)}\{Z_{i}^{(k)}\} is conditionally i.i.d. given {xi}\{x_{i}\} and independent of the queries across ii. The joint distribution of (W1,…,Wn+1)(W_{1},\ldots,W_{n+1}) is therefore invariant under any permutation π\pi of {1,…,n+1}\{1,\ldots,n+1\}: permuting the indices re-labels the exchangeable queries and correspondingly re-labels their (conditionally i.i.d.) Monte-Carlo draws, leaving the joint distribution unchanged. Because sk​(xi,ytrue(i))=f⁡(Wi)s_{k}(x_{i},y_{\mathrm{true}}^{(i)})=f(W_{i}) and ff is a fixed measurable function applied coordinate-wise, the score vector (sk​(x1,ytrue(1)),…,sk​(xn+1,ytrue(n+1)))(s_{k}(x_{1},y_{\mathrm{true}}^{(1)}),\ldots,s_{k}(x_{n+1},y_{\mathrm{true}}^{(n+1)})) inherits the same permutation invariance, which is the definition of exchangeability. ∎

Lemma 5 certifies that the split conformal machinery (Theorem 1) applies to the frequency score without modification. The argument extends to any nonconformity score that is a fixed measurable function of (x,a)(x,a) and a conditionally i.i.d. randomization; in particular, logprob-based scores of the form s⁡(x,a)=1−pk​(a∣x)s(x,a)=1-p_{k}(a\mid x) (where pk​(a∣x)p_{k}(a\mid x) is itself estimated from NN draws) are covered by the same argument.

Caveat: shared randomness across queries.

Lemma 5 assumes that the Monte Carlo draws {Zi(k)}\{Z_{i}^{(k)}\} are independent across queries. Production LLM serving stacks sometimes introduce per-query dependencies that can violate this: shared KV-cache prefixes across queries that happen to be batched together, or deterministic seeding that reuses randomness across queries. When those dependencies exist, the exchangeability argument needs to be re-examined. In our experiments we draw each query’s NN samples independently (standard vLLM behaviour at non-zero temperature with per-query seeds), so the assumption is satisfied.

Cross-tier correlation of calibration scores.

The calibration queries (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}) are shared across tiers k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K, but the Monte Carlo draws {Zi(k)}i\{Z_{i}^{(k)}\}_{i} and hence the scores {sk​(xi,yi)}i\{s_{k}(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i} are tier-specific. Theorem 2’s proof only uses the per-tier marginal coverage guarantee and is therefore unaffected by cross-tier score correlation. The cascade’s overall behaviour (which tier commits) does depend on the joint tier-11 through tier-kk thresholds, but that dependence is captured in the accounting of the first-commit events {Ak}\{A_{k}\}, not in the CP guarantee at each tier.

Resolution of the frequency score.

The score sk​(x,a)s_{k}(x,a) takes at most N+1N+1 distinct values, namely {0,1/N,2/N,…,1}\{0,1/N,2/N,\ldots,1\}, because the numerator is an integer in {0,…,N}\{0,\ldots,N\}. The calibrated quantile q^k\hat{q}_{k} is a specific order statistic of these scores and therefore also takes values on the same grid. At N=16N=16 (our default), the per-query resolution is 1/16≈0.0631/16\approx 0.063, which means the conformal threshold can be placed at one of 17 discrete levels per tier. This is enough to discriminate confident from uncertain queries while keeping inference inexpensive; if sharper prediction sets are needed, increasing NN linearly refines the grid but also scales per-query inference cost linearly.

Comparison to logprob-based scores.

When logprobs are available (e.g., in open-weight inference or some API endpoints), the continuous score sk​(x,a)=1−pk​(a∣x)s_{k}(x,a)=1-p_{k}(a\mid x) produces prediction sets whose conformal thresholds are not restricted to a discrete grid, and therefore yields tighter sets at the same α\alpha. We default to the frequency score because it preserves the black-box API interface assumed by many production deployments. The method in Section 3 is otherwise agnostic to the score choice: any valid nonconformity score composes with Algorithm 1.

L.2 Calibration Details

Computational cost.

For each tier kk, calibration performs nn calls to mkm_{k} (drawing NN samples per call) and then sorts the nn resulting scores. The sort is O⁡(n​log⁡n)O(n\log n) time and O⁡(n)O(n) space; subsequent inference uses q^k\hat{q}_{k} via a single O⁡(1)O(1) lookup. Across KK tiers, the full calibration cost is K⋅n⋅NK\cdot n\cdot N inference calls plus O⁡(K​n​log⁡n)O(Kn\log n) arithmetic, which is dominated by the inference budget.

Calibration-set size.

The calibration size nn controls the upper-side slack in Theorem 1: coverage lies in [1−α, 1−α+1/(n+1)][1-\alpha,\,1-\alpha+1/(n+1)]. With our default n=0.3⋅|benchmark|n=0.3\cdot|\mathrm{benchmark}|, the slack is at most 0.020.02 on all benchmarks with |benchmark|≥50|\mathrm{benchmark}|\geq 50, which includes every benchmark we evaluate except the smallest (AGI-Eval at n≈54n\approx 54 calibration queries, with slack ≈0.018\approx 0.018, and GPQA-Diamond at n≈59n\approx 59, with slack ≈0.017\approx 0.017). For fresh deployments, we recommend n≥200n\geq 200 calibration queries, giving slack ≤0.005\leq 0.005.

Tie-breaking.

When the calibration scores contain ties at the quantile index, we break ties by preserving sort order. This is the conservative convention: it slightly enlarges the prediction sets relative to randomized tie-breaking, which strengthens the coverage lower bound at the cost of minor set-size inflation.

L.3 Proof of Theorem 2 and Additional Remarks

Proof of Theorem 2.

Partition the acceptance event AA into the KK disjoint first-commit events Ak={K∗(x)=k}A_{k}=\{K^{*}(x)=k\} for k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K, so A=⨆k=1KAkA=\bigsqcup_{k=1}^{K}A_{k}. On the event AkA_{k}, Algorithm 1 returns y^\hat{y} equal to the unique element of 𝒞k​(x)\mathcal{C}_{k}(x). Therefore the error event intersected with AkA_{k},

Ak∩{y^≠ytrue}=Ak∩{𝒞k(x)∌ytrue}⊆{ytrue∉𝒞k(x)}.A_{k}\cap\{\hat{y}\neq y_{\mathrm{true}}\}\;=\;A_{k}\cap\{\mathcal{C}_{k}(x)\not\ni y_{\mathrm{true}}\}\;\subseteq\;\{y_{\mathrm{true}}\notin\mathcal{C}_{k}(x)\}.

By the per-tier split conformal guarantee at tier kk (Theorem 1, applicable by Lemma 5), Pr[ytrue∉𝒞k(x)]≤α\mathrm{Pr}[y_{\mathrm{true}}\notin\mathcal{C}_{k}(x)]\leq\alpha. Monotonicity of probability gives

Pr[y^≠ytrue,Ak]≤Pr[ytrue∉𝒞k(x)]≤α.\mathrm{Pr}[\hat{y}\neq y_{\mathrm{true}},\,A_{k}]\;\leq\;\mathrm{Pr}[y_{\mathrm{true}}\notin\mathcal{C}_{k}(x)]\;\leq\;\alpha.

Summing over kk and using the disjointness of {Ak}k=1K\{A_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K},

Pr⁡[y^≠ytrue,A]=∑k=1KPr⁡[y^≠ytrue,Ak]≤∑k=1Kα=K​α.\mathrm{Pr}[\hat{y}\neq y_{\mathrm{true}},\,A]\;=\;\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{Pr}[\hat{y}\neq y_{\mathrm{true}},\,A_{k}]\;\leq\;\sum_{k=1}^{K}\alpha\;=\;K\alpha.

This establishes (5). The final equivalence (per-tier level α/K\alpha/K gives cascade error α\alpha) is immediate by substitution. ∎

Remark 6 (Tightness of the union bound and selection preservation).

The factor KK in (5) is a worst-case union bound. In practice, the events {ytrue∉𝒞k(x)}∩{K∗(x)=k}\{y_{\mathrm{true}}\notin\mathcal{C}_{k}(x)\}\cap\{K^{*}(x)=k\} do not stack—most error mass at tier kk is not also error mass at other tiers. Assumption 3 in the main body formalizes this through the conditional bound

Pr[ytrue∈𝒞k(x)∣K∗(x)=k]≥ 1−α,for each k=1,…,K,\mathrm{Pr}[y_{\mathrm{true}}\in\mathcal{C}_{k}(x)\mid K^{*}(x)=k]\;\geq\;1-\alpha,\qquad\text{for each }k=1,\ldots,K,

under which the conditional cascade-error bound Pr⁡[y^≠ytrue∣A]≤α\mathrm{Pr}[\hat{y}\neq y_{\mathrm{true}}\mid A]\leq\alpha holds without the factor of KK.

The assumption is in the family studied by the selective-conformal literature (Bates et al., 2023; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2023; Foygel Barber et al., 2021), which treats coverage preservation under selection rules that depend on the calibration and test covariates but not on the test label. In our setting, the first-commit event {K∗(x)=k}\{K^{*}(x)=k\} is indeed measurable with respect to (x,𝒟cal)(x,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}}) alone and does not touch ytruey_{\mathrm{true}}, so the assumption is plausible in principle. It is not, however, a theorem of split conformal prediction without further regularity on the score distribution, and the cascade literature has not to our knowledge established sufficient conditions for it to hold identically in the multi-tier setting.

Empirical evidence for the assumption in this paper is indirect. Section 5.3 (Table 2) and Appendix I (Table 10) report the marginal set-miscoverage rate Pr[ytrue∉𝒞K∗​(x)(x)]\mathrm{Pr}[y_{\mathrm{true}}\notin\mathcal{C}_{K^{*}(x)}(x)] across the reported benchmark–family pairs. The marginal rate tracks α\alpha rather than the worst-case K​αK\alpha; on benchmarks with a substantial tier-1 acceptance rate (Section 5.5), this observation rules out the possibility that the bound K​αK\alpha is tight in our setting. We do not report the conditional rate Pr⁡[ytrue∉𝒞k​(x)∣K∗​(x)=k]\mathrm{Pr}[y_{\mathrm{true}}\notin\mathcal{C}_{k}(x)\mid K^{*}(x)=k] directly in this version of the paper; a future version could include a per-tier conditional miscoverage breakdown for stronger direct evidence.

Remark 7 (Deferral never errs).

Only the acceptance event can commit a wrong answer: when the cascade defers at tier kk, the query is passed to tier k+1k+1 with no claim made, and the error accounting in Theorem 2 sums only over commit events {A1,…,AK}\{A_{1},\ldots,A_{K}\}. Escalation therefore incurs only additional cost, never coverage violation.

Remark 8 (Relaxed acceptance, κ>1\kappa>1).

For κ>1\kappa>1, the acceptance event becomes Aκ={1≤|𝒞K∗​(x)(x)|≤κ}A_{\kappa}=\{1\leq|\mathcal{C}_{K^{*}(x)}(x)|\leq\kappa\}, and the cascade returns y^=arg⁡mina∈𝒞K∗​(x)​(x)​sK∗​(x)​(x,a)\hat{y}=\arg\min_{a\in\mathcal{C}_{K^{*}(x)}(x)}s_{K^{*}(x)}(x,a). The set-coverage guarantee carries through: Pr⁡[ytrue∈𝒞K∗​(x)​(x),Aκ]≤K​α\mathrm{Pr}[y_{\mathrm{true}}\in\mathcal{C}_{K^{*}(x)}(x),A_{\kappa}]\leq K\alpha (or ≤α\leq\alpha under selection preservation) with |𝒞K∗​(x)​(x)|≤κ|\mathcal{C}_{K^{*}(x)}(x)|\leq\kappa. The top-1 error is bounded by the set-coverage miss plus the probability that the arg⁡min\arg\min tiebreaker selects a wrong element from a set that contains the correct answer; the latter quantity is bounded by (κ−1)/κ(\kappa-1)/\kappa in the worst case but is typically much smaller when the frequency ranking is informative.

Remark 9 (Heterogeneous per-tier levels αk\alpha_{k}).

Theorem 2 uses a common level α\alpha at every tier, but the same argument extends to heterogeneous levels α1,…,αK\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{K}: the cascade-level error is bounded by ∑k=1Kαk\sum_{k=1}^{K}\alpha_{k} (or maxk⁡αk\max_{k}\alpha_{k} under selection preservation). Practitioners who want a tighter guarantee at later tiers, where escalation cost is already sunk, can choose α1>α2>⋯>αK\alpha_{1}>\alpha_{2}>\cdots>\alpha_{K} to concentrate the coverage budget on deeper commits.

L.4 Proof of Theorem 4 and Cost Results

Proof of Theorem 4.

By Algorithm 1 with K=2K=2 and κ=1\kappa=1: when |𝒞1​(X)|=1|\mathcal{C}_{1}(X)|=1 the cascade accepts at tier 1 and pays c1c_{1}; otherwise it escalates to tier 2 and pays c1+c2c_{1}+c_{2} (tier-1 samples are drawn regardless). Linearity of expectation gives

𝔼[Cost(X)]=c1⋅Pr[|𝒞1(X)|=1]+(c1+c2)⋅Pr[|𝒞1(X)|≠1]=c1+c2⋅Pr[|𝒞1(X)|≠1].\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}(X)]\;=\;c_{1}\cdot\mathrm{Pr}[|\mathcal{C}_{1}(X)|=1]+(c_{1}+c_{2})\cdot\mathrm{Pr}[|\mathcal{C}_{1}(X)|\neq 1]\;=\;c_{1}+c_{2}\cdot\mathrm{Pr}[|\mathcal{C}_{1}(X)|\neq 1].

The asymptotic limits follow from the monotonicity of the calibrated threshold q^1\hat{q}_{1} in α\alpha: as α→0\alpha\to 0, the quantile index ⌈(1−α)​(n+1)⌉→n+1\lceil(1-\alpha)(n+1)\rceil\to n+1, pushing q^1\hat{q}_{1} toward maxi⁡si(1)\max_{i}s_{i}^{(1)}; prediction sets then grow and the probability of a non-singleton set tends to 11. As α→1\alpha\to 1, the quantile index tends to 00, q^1\hat{q}_{1} tends to the minimum score value, prediction sets shrink to the singleton of each query’s argmin-score answer, and Pr[|𝒞1(X)|≠1]→0\mathrm{Pr}[|\mathcal{C}_{1}(X)|\neq 1]\to 0. ∎

Proposition 10 (When the cascade saves cost).

𝔼⁡[Cost⁡(X)]<c1+c2\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}(X)]<c_{1}+c_{2} if and only if Pr[|𝒞1(X)|=1]>0\mathrm{Pr}[|\mathcal{C}_{1}(X)|=1]>0, i.e., the cheap model produces at least some singleton prediction sets under calibration.

Proof.

By (6), 𝔼[Cost(X)]=c1+c2−c2⋅Pr[|𝒞1(X)|=1]\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}(X)]=c_{1}+c_{2}-c_{2}\cdot\mathrm{Pr}[|\mathcal{C}_{1}(X)|=1]. Since c2>0c_{2}>0, the expected cost is strictly below c1+c2c_{1}+c_{2} iff Pr[|𝒞1(X)|=1]>0\mathrm{Pr}[|\mathcal{C}_{1}(X)|=1]>0. ∎

Corollary 11 (KK-tier cost).

For a KK-tier cascade with costs c1<⋯<cKc_{1}<\cdots<c_{K} and κ=1\kappa=1, let pk=Pr[K∗(X)=k]p_{k}=\mathrm{Pr}[K^{*}(X)=k] denote the probability of first-commit at tier kk (with pKp_{K} absorbing fallback events). Then

𝔼⁡[Cost⁡(X)]=∑k=1K(∑j=1kcj)⋅pk.\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}(X)]\;=\;\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{k}c_{j}\right)\cdot p_{k}. (7)

Each pkp_{k} is determined by the per-tier thresholds q^1,…,q^K\hat{q}_{1},\ldots,\hat{q}_{K} and is estimable on calibration data.

Proof of Corollary 11.

Partition the space by the first-commit tier K∗​(X)∈{1,…,K}K^{*}(X)\in\{1,\ldots,K\}, which is exhaustive and disjoint. On the event {K∗(X)=k}\{K^{*}(X)=k\} the cascade has run tiers 1,…,k1,\ldots,k, so the incurred cost is ∑j=1kcj\sum_{j=1}^{k}c_{j}. Linearity of expectation yields

𝔼[Cost(X)]=∑k=1K(∑j=1kcj)Pr[K∗(X)=k],\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}(X)]\;=\;\sum_{k=1}^{K}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{k}c_{j}\right)\mathrm{Pr}[K^{*}(X)=k],

which is (7) with pk=Pr[K∗(X)=k]p_{k}=\mathrm{Pr}[K^{*}(X)=k]. Each pkp_{k} depends only on the per-tier thresholds q^1,…,q^k\hat{q}_{1},\ldots,\hat{q}_{k} and is thus estimable from the calibration set without further labels on test queries. ∎

Remark 12 (Deployment recipe for choosing α\alpha under a target error rate).

Fix a target cascade error rate β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1). The coverage bound of Theorem 2 restricts the admissible per-tier levels to the interval (0,β/K](0,\beta/K]; under Assumption 3 the admissible interval widens to (0,β](0,\beta]. Within either interval we recommend the upper endpoint — α=β/K\alpha=\beta/K in the worst case, α=β\alpha=\beta under selection preservation — as a deployment heuristic, on the grounds that larger α\alpha produces tighter per-tier thresholds, more singleton tier-1 sets, and lower expected cost.

This is a heuristic, not a theorem. The argument below establishes monotonicity of 𝔼⁡[Cost⁡(X)]\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}(X)] in α\alpha up to an O⁡(γ)O(\gamma) slack controlled by the empty-set probability γ=maxkPr[|𝒞k(X;α)|=0]\gamma=\max_{k}\mathrm{Pr}[|\mathcal{C}_{k}(X;\alpha)|=0], which vanishes only asymptotically in the per-query sample size NN. At finite NN (we use N=16N=16), strict monotonicity is not guaranteed, so the heuristic recipe should be validated by sweeping α\alpha on calibration data and inspecting the cost curve before deployment. We do this sweep for α∈{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20,0.30}\alpha\in\{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20,0.30\} (Appendix J); the curve is monotone on every reported benchmark–family pair in the regime α≤0.30\alpha\leq 0.30.

Justification of Remark 12.

Admissibility follows from Theorem 2: for cascade error at most β\beta, per-tier level α\alpha must satisfy K​α≤βK\alpha\leq\beta, so α∈(0,β/K]\alpha\in(0,\beta/K] in the worst case; the corresponding statement under Assumption 3 is immediate.

We sketch the asymptotic monotonicity claim. Define the non-empty regime at tolerance γ\gamma as the set of α\alpha values for which Pr[|𝒞k(X;α)|=0]≤γ\mathrm{Pr}[|\mathcal{C}_{k}(X;\alpha)|=0]\leq\gamma for every tier kk. For the frequency score with NN samples per query, empty sets occur only at q^k<1/N\hat{q}_{k}<1/N, which corresponds to α\alpha close to 11; at N=16N=16, the non-empty regime at γ=0.05\gamma=0.05 covers α≲0.9\alpha\lesssim 0.9 on the benchmarks we evaluate.

Within the non-empty regime, fix α1<α2\alpha_{1}<\alpha_{2}. The quantile index ⌈(1−α)​(n+1)⌉\lceil(1-\alpha)(n+1)\rceil is non-increasing in α\alpha, so q^k​(α1)≥q^k​(α2)\hat{q}_{k}(\alpha_{1})\geq\hat{q}_{k}(\alpha_{2}) at each tier kk and 𝒞k​(x,α1)⊇𝒞k​(x,α2)\mathcal{C}_{k}(x;\alpha_{1})\supseteq\mathcal{C}_{k}(x;\alpha_{2}) pointwise. Writing pk⋆(α)=Pr[|𝒞k(X;α)|=1]p_{k}^{\star}(\alpha)=\mathrm{Pr}[|\mathcal{C}_{k}(X;\alpha)|=1] and pk∅(α)=Pr[|𝒞k(X;α)|=0]p_{k}^{\emptyset}(\alpha)=\mathrm{Pr}[|\mathcal{C}_{k}(X;\alpha)|=0], set inclusion gives

pk⋆​(α2)≥pk⋆​(α1)−(pk∅​(α2)−pk∅​(α1)),p_{k}^{\star}(\alpha_{2})\;\geq\;p_{k}^{\star}(\alpha_{1})-\bigl(p_{k}^{\emptyset}(\alpha_{2})-p_{k}^{\emptyset}(\alpha_{1})\bigr),

so pk⋆p_{k}^{\star} is non-decreasing in α\alpha up to an O⁡(γ)O(\gamma) slack on the non-empty regime. Plugging into Corollary 11 yields 𝔼⁡[Cost⁡(X,α2)]≤𝔼⁡[Cost⁡(X,α1)]+O⁡(γ​∑kck)\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}(X;\alpha_{2})]\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}(X;\alpha_{1})]+O(\gamma\sum_{k}c_{k}). The slack γ\gamma vanishes as N→∞N\to\infty whenever the cheap model places non-vanishing mass on at least one answer per query, so strict monotonicity, and the minimum at α=β/K\alpha=\beta/K, hold asymptotically. At finite NN the slack persists, which is why we frame the claim as a deployment heuristic rather than a theorem; the calibration sweep in Appendix J provides the finite-NN certificate. ∎

L.5 Computational Complexity

Every stage of Conformal Cascade has transparent cost, and the overhead introduced by conformal calibration is dominated by the LLM inference calls a cascade must make anyway.

Calibration.

At tier kk, calibration processes nn queries by drawing NN Monte Carlo samples per query (amortized against self-consistency decoding) and computing the true-answer frequency score. The conformal quantile q^k\hat{q}_{k} is then a single sort over nn scores, at O⁡(n​log⁡n)O(n\log n) time and O⁡(n)O(n) space per tier. The full calibration over KK tiers is K⋅n⋅NK\cdot n\cdot N inference calls plus O⁡(K​n​log⁡n)O(Kn\log n) for the sorts, dominated entirely by the inference cost.

Inference.

For a new query xx, the cascade draws NN samples from each tier mkm_{k} up to and including the committed tier K∗​(x)K^{*}(x), computes sk​(x,a)s_{k}(x,a) for each a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} (an |𝒜||\mathcal{A}|-way tally over the NN samples), and constructs 𝒞k​(x)\mathcal{C}_{k}(x) by comparing each score against q^k\hat{q}_{k}. The dominant cost is LLM inference: at worst K⋅NK\cdot N calls with per-call costs c1,c2,…,cKc_{1},c_{2},\ldots,c_{K} growing geometrically. The remaining operations—the tally, the threshold comparisons, and the argmin over 𝒞k​(x)\mathcal{C}_{k}(x)—are O⁡(|𝒜|)O(|\mathcal{A}|) and negligible relative to LLM inference. When the cascade accepts at tier 1, only NN cheap-model calls are incurred per query, which is the regime that makes cascades cost-effective in the first place.

Memory.

Persistent state beyond the base cascade is the KK calibrated thresholds q^1,…,q^K\hat{q}_{1},\ldots,\hat{q}_{K}, i.e., KK scalars per cascade.

Summary.

The conformal wrapper adds no asymptotic overhead on top of a base self-consistency cascade: calibration runs once and produces KK scalars; inference reuses samples that self-consistency already requires. This makes CC a drop-in replacement for heuristic deferral rules: the additional computation is linear in the calibration-set size, constant per query, and dominated by LLM inference costs that the cascade was already paying.

L.6 Tightness of the Base Conformal Bound

Proposition 13 (Marginal-coverage upper bound).

Under the exchangeability assumption of Theorem 1, and assuming the calibration scores {s⁡(xi,yi)}i=1n\{s(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} are almost-surely distinct, split conformal prediction satisfies

1−α≤Pr[ytrue∈𝒞(xn+1)]≤ 1−α+1n+1.1-\alpha\;\leq\;\mathrm{Pr}[y_{\mathrm{true}}\in\mathcal{C}(x_{n+1})]\;\leq\;1-\alpha+\frac{1}{n+1}.

The upper bound follows from standard conformal analysis (Vovk et al., 2005; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2023): the probability that the test score exceeds the ⌈(1−α)​(n+1)⌉\lceil(1-\alpha)(n+1)\rceil-th order statistic of the calibration scores is at most ⌊α⁡(n+1)⌋/(n+1)≤α\lfloor\alpha(n+1)\rfloor/(n+1)\leq\alpha, and correspondingly the coverage is at most 1−α+1/(n+1)1-\alpha+1/(n+1). The two bounds together sandwich the coverage in a 1/(n+1)1/(n+1)-wide interval, which sharpens as the calibration set grows.

Caveat under discrete scores.

The almost-sure-distinct hypothesis is essential for the upper bound, not the lower bound. Our frequency score sks_{k} takes values on the discrete grid {0,1/N,…,1}\{0,1/N,\ldots,1\} at N=16N=16 (Section L.1, “Resolution of the frequency score”), so calibration scores tie with positive probability and the hypothesis fails. The lower bound Pr[ytrue∈𝒞(xn+1)]≥1−α\mathrm{Pr}[y_{\mathrm{true}}\in\mathcal{C}(x_{n+1})]\geq 1-\alpha continues to hold because the conservative tie-breaking convention in Section L.2 only enlarges prediction sets. The upper bound, however, can fail: ties at the quantile push extra probability mass into the prediction set, so the realised coverage may exceed 1−α+1/(n+1)1-\alpha+1/(n+1). This is the standard behaviour of split CP under discrete scores and explains why our reported set-miscoverage rates (Section 5.3) sometimes lie strictly below α\alpha rather than tracking the upper edge.
